screens.title: Python's role in network automation
screens.narratorSegment: Python’s popularity in network automation comes from three practical traits: simple readable syntax, a large set of libraries, and a low barrier to entry for engineers. Readable syntax means network engineers who are not formal software developers can inspect and maintain scripts; a one-line print or assignment communicates intent quickly. The rich ecosystem — including requests and json — gives you ready-made tools for HTTP interactions and data parsing so you don’t implement low-level protocols yourself. Concretely, consider a repetitive task such as auditing interface status across ten routers: a few lines of Python can fetch each device's RESTCONF interface list, parse operational state, and produce a compact report. A common misconception is that Python is too slow or heavyweight for network tasks; for control-plane automation and A P I orchestration the execution speed is rarely the bottleneck—network input and output and A P I latency dominate. The key takeaway is that Python is glue: it connects CLI, APIs, and orchestration platforms with minimal ceremony. Try describing one manual task in your environment and imagine the script that would replace it — that thought experiment reveals immediate automation opportunities.

content.html:
Core Concept Python's role
Definition

Python is a high-level interpreted language used to automate network tasks because it is readable and has libraries for HTTP and JSON handling. It lets engineers script device interactions without deep software-engineering overhead.

Example
Automating an interface audit: fetch interface lists from devices and produce a CSV of operational status.
Misconception
Python is not too slow for automation tasks that are I/O bound; network latency usually dominates runtime.
Key Takeaway

Python is the practical tool for gluing APIs, CLI, and orchestration into repeatable automation.

Analogy & scenario

Think of Python as the administrative script that checks rooms on a campus. Each room is a device, the list of rooms is a list, and the script reports rooms that need attention. Similarly, Python iterates devices, queries status, and reports discrepancies.

Try this
Write three lines: assign a hostname string, a list of two interface names, and a dictionary with a hostname and IP. Print each one to confirm structure.

screens.title: Variables and core data types
screens.narratorSegment: Variables in Python are named references to values; you do not declare types explicitly — Python infers them. Use a string to hold hostnames or interface descriptions, a list to hold ordered collections like multiple interfaces, and a dictionary to represent structured device data with named fields such as hostname and ip. For example, a hostname assignment is simply a string variable, while an interfaces list might contain the interface names you iterate over. A device_info dictionary maps keys like hostname and ip to their values and mirrors the JSON you’ll get from RESTCONF. A common pitfall is mutating a string thinking it behaves like a list; strings are immutable, while lists are mutable. Another mistake is treating dictionary access as guaranteed; direct key access raises an error if the key is absent. Prefer using. get() when working with A P I-derived dictionaries to avoid KeyError. Practice creating each type, printing its type, and performing a small operation: append an interface to a list, read a dictionary key safely, and slice a string for a short description. These simple operations form the building blocks for parsing A P I responses reliably.

content.html:
Definition Variables & Types
Code examples
device_ip = "192.168.1.10"
hostname = "Router1"
interfaces = ["GigabitEthernet1", "GigabitEthernet2"]
device_info = {"hostname": "Router1", "ip": "192.168.1.10"}
# Modify the list
interfaces.append("GigabitEthernet3")
# Safe dictionary access
name = device_info.get("hostname")
print(name)
These short lines mirror typical data you’ll receive from APIs.
Explanation & common mistakes
  • Strings are immutable; lists are mutable and useful for sequences of interfaces.
  • Dictionaries model structured JSON; prefer .get() to avoid exceptions when keys are missing.
  • Use type-checks sparingly; trust Python’s dynamic typing but validate external data.
Pro Tip

When building lists of interfaces from an API, normalize names before appending to reduce duplicates.

screens.title: Control flow: conditionals and loops
screens.narratorSegment: Control flow lets a script react to device state and repeat actions. Use if/else to check conditions such as whether an interface oper-status equals up, and use for loops to iterate over lists of VLANs, interfaces, or device IPs. Concretely, a loop over a list of VLAN IDs can send the same configuration or check to each VLAN; a loop over a devices dictionary with items() returns device name and IP to operate on. A common mistake is modifying a list while iterating it; prefer building a new list or iterating a shallow copy. Another pitfall is over-nesting conditionals — refactor repeated logic into functions to keep code readable. Practice by writing a for loop that prints formatting lines for each interface and an if/else that prints an actionable message when an interface is down. Remember to handle empty collections: a for loop over an empty list simply does nothing, so explicitly check and report when no interfaces are returned from an A P I. That small check prevents silent failures in automation runs. Control flow: conditionals and loops means if/else makes decisions; for loops repeat actions. avoid mutating lists while iterating and handle empty results explicitly.. In practical terms, make decisions and repeat work across devices and interfaces. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Process Flow If / For
If / Else example
interface_status = "up"
if interface_status == "up":
  print("Interface is operational.")
else:
  print("Interface is down.")
This conditional yields a clear action based on status.
For loop patterns
vlans = [10,20,30]
for vlan in vlans:
  print(f"Configuring VLAN {vlan}")

devices = {"R1": "192.168.1.1", "SW1": "192.168.1.2"}
for name, ip in devices.items():
  print(f"Device {name} has IP {ip}")
When iterating dicts, use .items() to access key-value pairs reliably.
Common mistake
Mutating the same list while iterating leads to skipped items; iterate a copy or collect changes separately.
Check your output
Always verify loops run at least once or handle zero-length lists explicitly to surface unexpected API results.

screens.title: Functions: modularity and reuse
screens.narratorSegment: Functions let you encapsulate repeated logic, name it, and reuse it across scripts or modules. A function accepts parameters and returns values; for example, a function that configures a VLAN could accept an id and a name and print or return a result. Using functions reduces duplication and improves readability when you need to call the same RESTCONF endpoint for many devices. When writing functions for network automation, design clear input and output shapes: accept device credentials and return parsed dictionaries or lists that downstream code can iterate over. Avoid functions that both perform side effects and return inconsistent types; prefer either returning structured data or performing an action. A common misconception is that functions add unnecessary indirection; in fact, small, well-named functions make automation easier to test and debug. Practice by refactoring a loop that prints interface names into a function that accepts the interfaces list and returns a list of formatted strings. This pattern will make your get_interfaces script easier to maintain. Functions: modularity and reuse means design functions with clear inputs and outputs to keep automation modular, testable, and reusable.. In practical terms, encapsulate repeated actions into reusable blocks. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Definition Functions
Simple function example
def configure_vlan(vlan_id, vlan_name):
  """Simulates configuring a VLAN."""
  print(f"VLAN {vlan_id} ({vlan_name}) configured.")

configure_vlan(10, "DATA")
Name functions for their action and keep side-effects consistent.
When to return data
  • Return parsed JSON as dictionaries so callers can inspect results.
  • Use exceptions or return codes for error signaling rather than printing inside the function.
  • Keep network calls isolated so you can unit test parsing logic with sample data.
Key Takeaway

Modular functions make scripts easier to read, test, and reuse across devices.

screens.title: Using the requests library
screens.narratorSegment: The requests library is the standard choice in Python for sending HTTP requests to RESTful APIs because it provides a simple, human-friendly A P I for GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, and DELETE methods. Start by installing it with pip in your environment. For device APIs you will commonly use GET to retrieve state and POST or PATCH to change configuration. Authentication is often basic HTTP; requests provides HTTPBasicAuth to add credentials cleanly. A critical security note: using verify=False disables SSL certificate verification and mirrors curl’s insecure option; it is useful in lab environments but unsafe in production. You should replace it with proper certificate validation in deployed scripts. Also wrap requests calls in try-except blocks and use response. raise_for_status() to turn HTTP error codes into exceptions you can handle. Practice by crafting a simple GET to a known endpoint, check for errors, and print a short success message. Building this habit keeps your automation predictable when devices are unreachable or return errors. Using the requests library means requests simplifies http interactions; always handle authentication, check responses, and avoid verify=false in production.. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Tooling requests library
Install & basic GET
Install requests with pip. Then call GET with optional headers and authentication. Always guard calls with try-except and response.raise_for_status().
import requests
from requests.auth import HTTPBasicAuth

response = requests.get(url, headers=headers, auth=HTTPBasicAuth(USER, PASS), verify=False)
response.raise_for_status()
Security & errors
  • Never hardcode credentials for production; use environment variables or a secrets manager.
  • verify=False is acceptable for labs only; validate certificates in production.
  • Wrap network calls to handle RequestException and JSON decoding errors cleanly.
Lab note
In the hands-on task you will use HTTPBasicAuth and verify=False for a lab device. Replace that before any production use.

keyIdea.text: GET, check status, parse JSON, and use .get() to access keys safely — repeat this pattern for other endpoints.

content.html:
Example Walkthrough GET hostname
Code snippet
import requests
import json
from requests.auth import HTTPBasicAuth
from requests.packages.urllib3.exceptions import InsecureRequestWarning
requests.packages.urllib3.disable_warnings(InsecureRequestWarning)

DEVICE_IP = "192.168.1.10"
USERNAME = "admin"
PASSWORD = "your_password"
url = f"https://{DEVICE_IP}/restconf/data/Cisco-IOS-XE-native:native/hostname"
headers = {"Accept": "application/yang-data+json"}

try:
  response = requests.get(url, headers=headers, auth=HTTPBasicAuth(USERNAME, PASSWORD), verify=False)
  response.raise_for_status()
  hostname_data = response.json()
  print(json.dumps(hostname_data, indent=2))
except requests.exceptions.RequestException as e:
  print(f"An error occurred: {e}")
Notes
  • Headers request YANG JSON; mismatch yields unexpected structures.
  • response.raise_for_status() surfaces 4xx/5xx errors early.
  • Pretty-print raw JSON for debugging, then parse specific keys with .get().
Misconception
Printing raw JSON is useful for debugging, but production scripts should parse and validate expected keys.

screens.title: Parsing JSON with the json module
screens.narratorSegment: The json module converts JSON strings into Python dictionaries and lists, and vice versa. content.html:
Hands-on Activity get_interfaces.py
Starter template
import requests
import json
from requests.auth import HTTPBasicAuth
from requests.packages.urllib3.exceptions import InsecureRequestWarning

# Suppress insecure request warning (for lab environments only)
requests.packages.urllib3.disable_warnings(InsecureRequestWarning)

# --- Configuration ---
DEVICE_IP = "YOUR_DEVICE_IP"
USERNAME = "YOUR_USERNAME"
PASSWORD = "YOUR_PASSWORD"
# ---------------------

def get_interface_status(device_ip, username, password):
  """Retrieves and prints the operational status of all interfaces."""
  url = f"https://{device_ip}/restconf/data/ietf-interfaces:interfaces/interface"
  headers = {"Accept": "application/yang-data+json"}
  try:
    response = requests.get(url, headers=headers, auth=HTTPBasicAuth(username, password), verify=False)
    response.raise_for_status()
    interface_data = response.json()
    interfaces = interface_data.get("ietf-interfaces:interfaces", {}).get("interface", [])
    if not interfaces:
      print("No interfaces found or unexpected data structure.")
      return
    for interface in interfaces:
      name = interface.get("name", "N/A")
      oper_status = interface.get("oper-status", "unknown")
      print(f"Interface: {name}, Status: {oper_status}")
  except requests.exceptions.RequestException as e:
    print(f"An error occurred: {e}")
  except json.JSONDecodeError:
    print("Failed to decode JSON response.")

if __name__ == "__main__":
  get_interface_status(DEVICE_IP, USERNAME, PASSWORD)
Checklist
  • Replace the configuration placeholders for your device.
  • Run the script and observe interface names and statuses in the terminal.
  • Uncomment raw JSON print to debug structure if parsing fails.
Security reminder
Do not leave verify=False or hardcoded credentials in production code.

screens.title: Common mistakes and defensive coding
screens.narratorSegment: When writing automation, several common mistakes can make scripts brittle or insecure. First, hardcoding credentials in a script can leak secrets; instead, use environment variables or a config file with appropriate permissions. Second, using direct dictionary access risks KeyError when keys are absent; prefer. get() with defaults and explicit checks for empty lists. Third, ignoring HTTP errors or JSON decoding exceptions causes scripts to fail silently; always call response. raise_for_status() and catch RequestException and JSONDecodeError. Fourth, using verify=False without planning leaves you open to man-in-the-middle risks; treat it as a lab-only convenience and switch to certificate validation for production. Finally, assuming a fixed JSON structure across device OS versions can break parsing; inspect raw responses during development and write parsers that tolerate missing fields. To defend against these issues, add explicit validation steps, log meaningful diagnostics for failed requests, and isolate network calls from parsing logic so you can test the parser with saved JSON fixtures. These practices shift automation from fragile scripts to reliable tools you can run repeatedly. Common mistakes and defensive coding means avoid hardcoded secrets, prefer .get(), handle network and json errors, and validate responses before parsing.. In practical terms, avoid fragile parsing and insecure practices. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

fullNarratorScript:
Python has become the practical choice for network automation because it balances readability with a rich ecosystem of libraries. In this lesson you will see how Python stores device information using variables, models collections with lists and dictionaries, makes decisions with control flow, and encapsulates work in functions. You will also learn how to use the requests library to call device RESTCONF endpoints and the built-in json module to parse A P I responses. These skills let you replace repetitive CLI tasks with repeatable scripts, such as fetching interface operational status across many devices. A concrete example you will build is a script that connects to a Cisco IOS XE RESTCONF A P I, retrieves interface data, and prints each interface name with its operational status. Along the way we’ll emphasize safe practices: using dictionary. get() calls to avoid KeyError, handling network exceptions gracefully, and never hardcoding secrets in production. By the end you will be able to read short Python scripts, adapt them to your devices, and write a small RESTCONF client that handles common errors. Consider this your toolkit for turning manual device checks into repeatable automation.

By the end of this chapter you will perform four concrete skills that matter in network automation. First, you will explain why Python is a good choice for network work, citing readability and library support, and you will give an example use case such as automating backups or querying device state. Second, you will write basic Python constructs: variables, strings, lists and dictionaries, and you will demonstrate converting an A P I response into those structures. Third, you will use control flow and functions to iterate over devices or interfaces safely, using loops and modular functions to avoid repetition. Fourth, you will call a device RESTCONF endpoint with the requests library, parse the JSON response with the json module, and safely access keys with. get() while handling errors. Each objective is a practical milestone; together they allow you to replace manual CLI checks with automated scripts that can be audited and repeated. Use these objectives as an applied checklist as you step through the hands-on activity.

This page breaks each learning objective into a practical verification step you can run in a lab. For explaining Python's role, prepare a brief note that lists a task you would automate and why Python suits it — a succinct justification helps during interviews and design meetings. For basic types, write three small lines of code that create a string for a hostname, a list of interfaces, and a dictionary representing device metadata, then print them. For control flow and functions, refactor a repetitive loop into a function that accepts a device IP and returns parsed results. For RESTCONF and JSON parsing, run a small script that uses requests. get() to fetch interface data, then use. get() to print name and oper-status for each interface, catching RequestException. Each verification builds confidence and maps directly to the hands-on activity. These are compact, repeatable checks that show you’ve internalized the skills and can apply them to real devices in your lab or a virtualized environment.

Python’s popularity in network automation comes from three practical traits: simple readable syntax, a large set of libraries, and a low barrier to entry for engineers. Readable syntax means network engineers who are not formal software developers can inspect and maintain scripts; a one-line print or assignment communicates intent quickly. The rich ecosystem — including requests and json — gives you ready-made tools for HTTP interactions and data parsing so you don’t implement low-level protocols yourself. Concretely, consider a repetitive task such as auditing interface status across ten routers: a few lines of Python can fetch each device's RESTCONF interface list, parse operational state, and produce a compact report. A common misconception is that Python is too slow or heavyweight for network tasks; for control-plane automation and A P I orchestration the execution speed is rarely the bottleneck—network input and output and A P I latency dominate. The key takeaway is that Python is glue: it connects CLI, APIs, and orchestration platforms with minimal ceremony. Try describing one manual task in your environment and imagine the script that would replace it — that thought experiment reveals immediate automation opportunities.

Variables in Python are named references to values; you do not declare types explicitly — Python infers them. Use a string to hold hostnames or interface descriptions, a list to hold ordered collections like multiple interfaces, and a dictionary to represent structured device data with named fields such as hostname and ip. For example, a hostname assignment is simply a string variable, while an interfaces list might contain the interface names you iterate over. A device_info dictionary maps keys like hostname and ip to their values and mirrors the JSON you’ll get from RESTCONF. A common pitfall is mutating a string thinking it behaves like a list; strings are immutable, while lists are mutable. Another mistake is treating dictionary access as guaranteed; direct key access raises an error if the key is absent. Prefer using. get() when working with A P I-derived dictionaries to avoid KeyError. Practice creating each type, printing its type, and performing a small operation: append an interface to a list, read a dictionary key safely, and slice a string for a short description. These simple operations form the building blocks for parsing A P I responses reliably.

Control flow lets a script react to device state and repeat actions. Use if/else to check conditions such as whether an interface oper-status equals up, and use for loops to iterate over lists of VLANs, interfaces, or device IPs. Concretely, a loop over a list of VLAN IDs can send the same configuration or check to each VLAN; a loop over a devices dictionary with items() returns device name and IP to operate on. A common mistake is modifying a list while iterating it; prefer building a new list or iterating a shallow copy. Another pitfall is over-nesting conditionals — refactor repeated logic into functions to keep code readable. Practice by writing a for loop that prints formatting lines for each interface and an if/else that prints an actionable message when an interface is down. Remember to handle empty collections: a for loop over an empty list simply does nothing, so explicitly check and report when no interfaces are returned from an A P I. That small check prevents silent failures in automation runs. Control flow: conditionals and loops means if/else makes decisions; for loops repeat actions. avoid mutating lists while iterating and handle empty results explicitly.. In practical terms, make decisions and repeat work across devices and interfaces. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Functions let you encapsulate repeated logic, name it, and reuse it across scripts or modules. A function accepts parameters and returns values; for example, a function that configures a VLAN could accept an id and a name and print or return a result. Using functions reduces duplication and improves readability when you need to call the same RESTCONF endpoint for many devices. When writing functions for network automation, design clear input and output shapes: accept device credentials and return parsed dictionaries or lists that downstream code can iterate over. Avoid functions that both perform side effects and return inconsistent types; prefer either returning structured data or performing an action. A common misconception is that functions add unnecessary indirection; in fact, small, well-named functions make automation easier to test and debug. Practice by refactoring a loop that prints interface names into a function that accepts the interfaces list and returns a list of formatted strings. This pattern will make your get_interfaces script easier to maintain. Functions: modularity and reuse means design functions with clear inputs and outputs to keep automation modular, testable, and reusable.. In practical terms, encapsulate repeated actions into reusable blocks. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

The requests library is the standard choice in Python for sending HTTP requests to RESTful APIs because it provides a simple, human-friendly A P I for GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, and DELETE methods. Start by installing it with pip in your environment. For device APIs you will commonly use GET to retrieve state and POST or PATCH to change configuration. Authentication is often basic HTTP; requests provides HTTPBasicAuth to add credentials cleanly. A critical security note: using verify=False disables SSL certificate verification and mirrors curl’s insecure option; it is useful in lab environments but unsafe in production. You should replace it with proper certificate validation in deployed scripts. Also wrap requests calls in try-except blocks and use response. raise_for_status() to turn HTTP error codes into exceptions you can handle. Practice by crafting a simple GET to a known endpoint, check for errors, and print a short success message. Building this habit keeps your automation predictable when devices are unreachable or return errors. Using the requests library means requests simplifies http interactions; always handle authentication, check responses, and avoid verify=false in production.. In practical terms, install, send http methods, and handle authentication. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

We will walk through a minimal RESTCONF GET that retrieves a device hostname. The code imports requests and json, configures authentication, disables warnings for lab SSL, and constructs a URL pointing to the native hostname path. The core call uses requests. get with headers that ask for yang-data+json. After the call, response. raise_for_status() converts HTTP errors into exceptions you can catch. Then response. json() returns a Python dictionary representing the returned JSON. A practical extraction uses the dictionary. get() method to retrieve the hostname key safely; if the key is absent. get() returns None, letting your code handle missing data without a KeyError. Mistakes to watch for: using the wrong Accept header, malformed URL paths, or forgetting to disable SSL verification only in labs. Use json. dumps with indentation to pretty-print raw responses when debugging, then switch to targeted parsing in production scripts. This example sets the pattern you'll reuse when querying other YANG model paths over RESTCONF. When writing automation, several common mistakes can make scripts brittle or insecure. First, hardcoding credentials in a script can leak secrets; instead, use environment variables or a config file with appropriate permissions. Second, using direct dictionary access risks KeyError when keys are absent; prefer. get() with defaults and explicit checks for empty lists. Third, ignoring HTTP errors or JSON decoding exceptions causes scripts to fail silently; always call response. raise_for_status() and catch RequestException and JSONDecodeError. Fourth, using verify=False without planning leaves you open to man-in-the-middle risks; treat it as a lab-only convenience and switch to certificate validation for production. Finally, assuming a fixed JSON structure across device OS versions can break parsing; inspect raw responses during development and write parsers that tolerate missing fields. To defend against these issues, add explicit validation steps, log meaningful diagnostics for failed requests, and isolate network calls from parsing logic so you can test the parser with saved JSON fixtures. These practices shift automation from fragile scripts to reliable tools you can run repeatedly.
